claim: Fusion of HIV-1 with the membrane of its target cell is an obligate first step in virus infectivity.
source: Fusion of HIV-1 with the membrane of its target cell, an obligate first step in virus infectivity, is mediated by binding of the viral envelope (Env) spike protein to its receptors, CD4 and CCR5/CXCR4, on the cell surface.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about HIV-1 infection mechanism.

claim: HIV-1 fusion with target cells is mediated by binding of the viral envelope (Env) spike protein to its receptors, CD4 and CCR5/CXCR4, on the cell surface.
source: Fusion of HIV-1 with the membrane of its target cell, an obligate first step in virus infectivity, is mediated by binding of the viral envelope (Env) spike protein to its receptors, CD4 and CCR5/CXCR4, on the cell surface.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about HIV-1 entry mechanism.

claim: The process of viral fusion appears to be fast compared with viral egress.
source: The process of viral fusion appears to be fast compared with viral egress and has not been visualized by EM.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that fusion has not been visualized by EM despite attempts.

claim: HIV-1 fusion has not been visualized by EM.
source: The process of viral fusion appears to be fast compared with viral egress and has not been visualized by EM.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of the field prior to this study.

claim: Fusion inhibitors can trap HIV-1 virions attached to target cells by Envs in an extended pre-hairpin intermediate state.
source: We have used fusion inhibitors to trap HIV-1 virions attached to target cells by Envs in an extended pre-hairpin intermediate state.
evidence: This is the primary experimental finding of the study, supported by the electron tomography data presented.

claim: Electron tomography revealed HIV-1 virions bound to TZM-bl cells by 2–4 narrow spokes.
source: Electron tomography revealed HIV-1 virions bound to TZM-bl cells by 2–4 narrow spokes, with slightly more spokes present when evaluated with mutant virions that lacked the Env cytoplasmic tail.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the electron tomography experiments presented in the manuscript.

claim: Slightly more spokes are present when evaluated with mutant virions that lacked the Env cytoplasmic tail.
source: Electron tomography revealed HIV-1 virions bound to TZM-bl cells by 2–4 narrow spokes, with slightly more spokes present when evaluated with mutant virions that lacked the Env cytoplasmic tail.
evidence: This is a direct observation from comparing wild-type and cytoplasmic tail-deleted virions in the experiments.

claim: This study represents the first direct visualization of the hypothesized pre-hairpin intermediate of HIV-1 Env.
source: These results represent the first direct visualization of the hypothesized pre-hairpin intermediate of HIV-1 Env and improve our understanding of Env-mediated HIV-1 fusion and infection of host cells.
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty of the findings, based on the experimental data presented.

claim: HIV-1 Env is a trimeric glycoprotein comprising three gp120 subunits that contain host receptor-binding sites and three gp41 subunits that include the fusion peptide and membrane-spanning regions.
source: HIV-1 Env is a trimeric glycoprotein comprising three gp120 subunits that contain host receptorbinding sites and three gp41 subunits that include the fusion peptide and membrane-spanning regions.
evidence: This is established structural knowledge about HIV-1 Env.

claim: Binding of the primary receptor CD4 to gp120 triggers conformational changes that expose a binding site for co-receptor (CCR5 or CXCR4).
source: Binding of the primary receptor CD4 to gp120 triggers conformational changes that expose a binding site for co-receptor (CCR5 or CXCR4).
evidence: This is established knowledge about the HIV-1 entry mechanism.

claim: Coreceptor binding results in conformational changes within gp41 that promote release of the hydrophobic fusion peptide, its insertion into the host cell membrane, and subsequent fusion of the host cell and viral membrane bilayers.
source: Coreceptor binding results in further conformational changes within gp41 that promote release of the hydrophobic fusion peptide, its insertion into the host cell membrane, and subsequent fusion of the host cell and viral membrane bilayers (Harrison, 2015).
evidence: This is established knowledge about HIV-1 fusion mechanism, supported by citation.

claim: X-ray and single-particle cryo-EM structures of soluble native-like Env trimers in the closed (pre-fusion) conformation have been determined.
source: Structural studies relevant to understanding Env-mediated membrane fusion include X-ray and single-particle cryo-EM structures of soluble native-like Env trimers in the closed (pre-fusion) conformation (Ward and Wilson, 2017)
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous structural studies.

claim: CD4-bound open trimers have been structurally characterized in which the co-receptor binding site on the third hypervariable loop (V3) of gp120 is exposed by V1V2 loop rearrangement.
source: CD4-bound open trimers in which the co-receptor binding site on the third hypervariable loop (V3) of gp120 is exposed by V1V2 loop rearrangement (Ozorowski et al., 2017; Wang et al., 2018; Wang et al., 2016; Yang et al., 2019)
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to structural studies.

claim: A gp120 monomeric core-CD4-CCR5 complex structure has been determined.
source: a gp120 monomeric core-CD4-CCR5 complex (Shaik et al., 2019)
evidence: This is supported by citation to a structural study.

claim: A post-fusion gp41 six-helical bundle is formed by an α-helical trimeric coiled coil from the gp41 N-trimer region surrounded by three helices from the C-peptide region.
source: a post-fusion gp41 six-helical bundle formed by an α-helical trimeric coiled coil from the gp41 N-trimer region surrounded by three helices from the C-peptide region (Chan et al., 1997; Weissenhorn et al., 1997; Figure 1a)
evidence: This is supported by citations to structural studies and illustrated in Figure 1a.

claim: Prior to membrane fusion and formation of the post-fusion gp41 helical bundle, the viral and host cell membranes are hypothesized to be linked by an extended pre-hairpin intermediate in which insertion of the gp41 fusion peptide into the host cell membrane exposes the N-trimer (HR1) region of gp41.
source: Prior to membrane fusion and formation of the post-fusion gp41 helical bundle, the viral and host cell membranes are hypothesized to be linked by an extended pre-hairpin intermediate in which insertion of the gp41 fusion peptide into the host cell membrane exposes the N-trimer (HR1) region of gp41 (Chan and Kim, 1998).
evidence: This is a hypothesis from the literature, supported by citation.

claim: Formation of the six-helical bundle and subsequent fusion can be inhibited by targeting the N-trimer region with C-peptide-based inhibitors.
source: Formation of the six-helical bundle and subsequent fusion can be inhibited by targeting the N-trimer region with C-peptide-based inhibitors; for example the fusion inhibitor T20 (enfuvirtide [Fuzeon]) (Kilgore et al., 2003), T1249, a more potent derivative of T20 (Eron et al., 2004), and a highly potent trimeric D-peptide (CPT31) (Redman et al., 2018), or with anti-gp41 antibodies such as D5 (Miller et al., 2005; Figure 1a).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by multiple citations and illustrated in Figure 1a.

claim: T20 (enfuvirtide [Fuzeon]) is a fusion inhibitor that targets the N-trimer region.
source: for example the fusion inhibitor T20 (enfuvirtide [Fuzeon]) (Kilgore et al., 2003)
evidence: This is supported by citation.

claim: T1249 is a more potent derivative of T20.
source: T1249, a more potent derivative of T20 (Eron et al., 2004)
evidence: This is supported by citation.

claim: CPT31 is a highly potent trimeric D-peptide fusion inhibitor.
source: a highly potent trimeric D-peptide (CPT31) (Redman et al., 2018)
evidence: This is supported by citation.

claim: D5 is an anti-gp41 antibody that can inhibit fusion.
source: or with anti-gp41 antibodies such as D5 (Miller et al., 2005; Figure 1a)
evidence: This is supported by citation and illustrated in Figure 1a.

claim: Despite 3-D imaging by electron tomography (ET) of HIV-1 infection of cultured cells, viruses caught in the act of fusion have not been unambiguously found.
source: Despite 3-D imaging by electron tomography (ET) of HIV-1 infection of cultured cells (Carlson et al., 2008; Carlson et al., 2010; Do et al., 2014; Earl et al., 2013) and tissues (Kieffer et al., 2017a; Kieffer et al., 2017b; Ladinsky et al., 2019; Ladinsky et al., 2014), viruses caught in the act of fusion have not been unambiguously found.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of the field, supported by citations to previous ET studies.

claim: In ET imaging of HIV-1–infected humanized mouse tissues, hundreds of budding virions at various stages of egress and thousands of free mature and immature virions have been identified, but not a single example of a virus attached to a host cell via a pre-hairpin intermediate or in the process of fusing its membrane with the target cell membrane.
source: In our ET imaging of HIV-1–infected humanized mouse tissues, we have identified hundreds of budding virions at various stages of egress and thousands of free mature and immature virions (Kieffer et al., 2017a; Kieffer et al., 2017b; Ladinsky et al., 2019; Ladinsky et al., 2014), but not a single example of a virus attached to a host cell via a pre-hairpin intermediate or in the process of fusing its membrane with the target cell membrane.
evidence: This is based on the authors' previous ET studies, supported by citations.

claim: The absence of observed viral fusion events might be explained if fusion is a fast process compared with viral budding.
source: The absence of observed viral fusion events might be explained if fusion is a fast process compared with viral budding; thus when cells or tissues are immobilized for EM or ET, the relatively slow process of viral budding would be more easily captured compared with the faster process of fusion.
evidence: This is a hypothesis to explain the lack of observed fusion events.

claim: When cells or tissues are immobilized for EM or ET, the relatively slow process of viral budding would be more easily captured compared with the faster process of fusion.
source: thus when cells or tissues are immobilized for EM or ET, the relatively slow process of viral budding would be more easily captured compared with the faster process of fusion.
evidence: This is an inference based on the relative rates of budding and fusion.

claim: Fusion could theoretically be observed if a virus were caught at exactly the right time, but this might require examining thousands or millions of images.
source: We assume that fusion could theoretically be observed if a virus were caught at exactly the right time, but this might require examining thousands or millions of images.
evidence: This is speculation about the difficulty of capturing fusion events.

claim: A previous study used ET to visualize HIV-1 and SIV virions in contact with target cells after promoting a temperature-arrested state.
source: A previous study used ET to visualize HIV-1 and SIV virions in contact with target cells after promoting a temperature-arrested state (Mkrtchyan et al., 2005) in which viruses can remain attached to cells prior to fusion (Sougrat et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: In the temperature-arrested state study, target cells were incubated with virus at 4°C to allow binding but not fusion, warmed to 37°C, and then fixed after incubations ranging from 15 min to 3 hr.
source: For that study, target cells were incubated with virus at 4°C to allow binding but not fusion, warmed to 37°C, and then fixed after incubations ranging from 15 min to 3 hr (Sougrat et al., 2007).
evidence: This describes the experimental protocol from a previous study, supported by citation.

claim: At all time points after warming in the temperature-arrested state study, viruses were found attached to target cells by a cluster of 5–7 'rods,' each ~100 Å long and ~100 Å wide.
source: At all time points after warming, viruses were found attached to target cells by a cluster of 5–7 'rods,' each ~100 Å long and ~100 Å wide.
evidence: This describes findings from a previous study.

claim: The attachment structure in the temperature-arrested state study was not found when the viruses and target cells were incubated in the presence of C34, a gp41 N-trimer–targeting C-peptide inhibitor related to T20.
source: The fact that the attachment structure was not found when the viruses and target cells were incubated in the presence of C34, a gp41 N-trimer–targeting C-peptide inhibitor related to T20 (Sougrat et al., 2007), suggests that the rod structure that was trapped during the temperature-arrested state did not involve the pre-hairpin intermediate.
evidence: This is based on findings from a previous study, supported by citation.

claim: The rod structure that was trapped during the temperature-arrested state did not involve the pre-hairpin intermediate.
source: The fact that the attachment structure was not found when the viruses and target cells were incubated in the presence of C34, a gp41 N-trimer–targeting C-peptide inhibitor related to T20 (Sougrat et al., 2007), suggests that the rod structure that was trapped during the temperature-arrested state did not involve the pre-hairpin intermediate.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that C34 prevented the attachment structure.

claim: Addition of an HIV-1 fusion inhibitor that binds to the exposed gp41 N-trimer after host cell receptor and coreceptor binding would slow or stop virus-host cell membrane fusion such that the pre-hairpin intermediate structures could be visualized by ET.
source: We hypothesized that addition of an HIV-1 fusion inhibitor that binds to the exposed gp41 N-trimer after host cell receptor and coreceptor binding would slow or stop virus-host cell membrane fusion such that we could visualize pre-hairpin intermediate structures by ET (Figure 1b).
evidence: This is the hypothesis that guided the experimental design of this study.

claim: T1249-Fc is a C-peptide–based inhibitor linked to human Fc with a molecular weight of 65 kDa.
source: We characterized three fusion inhibitors of different sizes and potencies that target the exposed gp41 N-trimer region of the pre-hairpin intermediate for attempts to visualize the pre-hairpin intermediate: T1249-Fc, a C-peptide–based inhibitor that we linked to human Fc (MW = 65 kDa)
evidence: This describes the fusion inhibitor used in the study.

claim: D5 IgG has a molecular weight of 150 kDa.
source: D5 IgG (MW = 150 kDa) (Miller et al., 2005)
evidence: This describes the fusion inhibitor used in the study, with citation.

claim: CPT31 is a high-affinity D-peptide inhibitor linked to cholesterol with a molecular weight of 9 kDa.
source: CPT31, a high-affinity D-peptide inhibitor linked to cholesterol (MW = 9 kDa) (Redman et al., 2018; Welch et al., 2010; Figure 1a; Figure 1—figure supplement 1a)
evidence: This describes the fusion inhibitor used in the study, with citations.

claim: Neutralization potencies of the fusion inhibitors were measured using in vitro HIV-1 pseudovirus neutralization assays against the SC4226618 and 6535 viral strains.
source: We measured their neutralization potencies using in vitro HIV-1 pseudovirus neutralization assays (Montefiori, 2009) against the SC4226618 and 6535 viral strains.
evidence: This describes the experimental method used to characterize the inhibitors.

claim: Potencies of the fusion inhibitors ranged from IC50 values of ~0.13 ng/mL for CPT31 to ≥40 µg/mL for D5 IgG.
source: We found potencies ranging from 50% inhibitory concentration (IC50) values of ~0.13 ng/mL for CPT31 to ≥40 µg/mL for D5 IgG (Figure 1—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: This is data from neutralization assays presented in the figure supplement.

claim: T1249-Fc exhibited intermediate potencies (IC50s = 0.99 µg/mL; 17 µg/mL).
source: T1249-Fc exhibited intermediate potencies (IC50s = 0.99 µg/mL; 17 µg/mL) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1a)
evidence: This is data from neutralization assays presented in the figure supplement.

claim: T1249-Fc exhibited higher IC50s than T1249 peptide alone, consistent with limited steric accessibility resulting in decreased potencies for larger fusion inhibitors.
source: T1249-Fc exhibited intermediate potencies (IC50s = 0.99 µg/mL; 17 µg/mL) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1a), higher than IC50s measured for T1249 peptide alone, consistent with limited steric accessibility resulting in decreased potencies for larger fusion inhibitors (Hamburger et al., 2005).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the data, supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Incubating with a fusion inhibitor at 37°C obviated the need for a 4°C incubation of virus and target cells.
source: Incubating with a fusion inhibitor at 37°C obviated the need for a 4°C incubation of virus and target cells, which we reasoned was desirable since low temperatures alter membrane fluidity (Avery et al., 1995; Simons and Vaz, 2004; Quinn, 1988), which could affect one or more steps in membrane fusion.
evidence: This is a rationale for the experimental design, supported by citations about membrane fluidity.

claim: Low temperatures alter membrane fluidity, which could affect one or more steps in membrane fusion.
source: which we reasoned was desirable since low temperatures alter membrane fluidity (Avery et al., 1995; Simons and Vaz, 2004; Quinn, 1988), which could affect one or more steps in membrane fusion.
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Target cells for HIV-1 are several microns in height, much thicker than the 0.5–1 µm limit for cryo-ET.
source: Since target cells for HIV-1 are several microns in height, much thicker than the 0.5–1 µm limit for cryo-ET (Beck and Baumeister, 2016), we used stained, plastic-embedded samples that could be cut into 300–400 nm sections using a microtome, and then examined the samples in 3-D using ET.
evidence: This is a rationale for the choice of sample preparation method, with citation about cryo-ET limits.

claim: ET of stained, plastic-embedded sections results in lower resolution than cryo-ET.
source: Although ET of stained, plastic-embedded sections results in lower resolution than cryo-ET, the minimal effects of radiation damage in plastic sections (Glaeser, 2016) was an advantage for locating rare attached virions.
evidence: This is established knowledge about ET methods, supported by citation.

claim: Plastic sections have minimal effects of radiation damage, which is an advantage for locating rare attached virions.
source: Although ET of stained, plastic-embedded sections results in lower resolution than cryo-ET, the minimal effects of radiation damage in plastic sections (Glaeser, 2016) was an advantage for locating rare attached virions.
evidence: This is a rationale for the choice of sample preparation method, supported by citation.

claim: More cells could be assayed in plastic sections than in samples prepared by cryo-ET methods, allowing for statistically significant observations of virion attachment events.
source: Thus, more cells could be assayed in plastic sections than in samples prepared by cryo-ET methods (e.g. by examining thin leading edges of cells or using focused-ion-beam milling [Villa et al., 2013] to prepare a sufficiently thin sample), therefore allowing for statistically significant observations of virion attachment events.
evidence: This is a rationale for the choice of sample preparation method.

claim: Samples were prepared by light fixation followed by high-pressure freezing/freeze substitution fixation (HPF-FSF).
source: We prepared samples by light fixation followed by high-pressure freezing/freeze substitution fixation (HPF-FSF) instead of the traditional chemical fixation protocol used previously (Sougrat et al., 2007)
evidence: This describes the sample preparation method used in the study.

claim: HPF vitrifies cells at ~10,000°/s, stopping all cellular movement within ms and allowing optimal preservation of ultrastructural features.
source: because HPF vitrifies cells at ~10,000°/s, stopping all cellular movement within ms and allowing optimal preservation of ultrastructural features (Kellenberger, 1991; McIntosh et al., 2005; Sartori et al., 1993; Dahl and Staehelin, 1989).
evidence: This is established knowledge about HPF, supported by multiple citations.

claim: Chemical fixation immobilizes elements in the cell at different rates, and movement and rearrangement of transmembrane proteins may continue even in the presence of aldehyde fixatives.
source: By contrast, chemical fixation immobilizes elements in the cell at different rates, and movement and rearrangement of transmembrane proteins may continue even in the presence of aldehyde fixatives (Brock et al., 1999; Stanly et al., 2016; Tanaka et al., 2010).
evidence: This is established knowledge about chemical fixation, supported by citations.

claim: Following HPF-FSF, samples were plastic embedded and stained with uranyl acetate and lead citrate.
source: Following HPF-FSF, samples were plastic embedded and stained with uranyl acetate and lead citrate as described in our previous ET studies of HIV-1 in infected tissues (Kieffer et al., 2017b; Ladinsky et al., 2019; Ladinsky et al., 2014).
evidence: This describes the sample preparation method, with citations to previous studies.

claim: The ultrastructure of HIV-1 pseudoviruses, including approximate numbers and dimensions of Env trimer spikes and the presence of collapsed (in mature virions) versus C-shaped (in immature virions) cores, was preserved during the fixation, embedding, and staining procedures.
source: we verified that the ultrastructure of HIV-1 pseudoviruses, including approximate numbers and dimensions of Env trimer spikes and the presence of collapsed (in mature virions) versus C-shaped (in immature virions) cores (Carlson et al., 2008; Benjamin et al., 2005; Ganser, 1999; Wright et al., 2007), was preserved during the fixation, embedding, and staining procedures (Figure 2—figure supplement 1a)
evidence: This is a verification of sample quality, supported by citations and shown in the figure supplement.

claim: TZM-bl cells are a HeLa cell line that stably expresses high levels of human CD4 and coreceptors CCR5 and CXCR4.
source: We conducted ET experiments by first incubating TZM-bl cells, a HeLa cell line that stably expresses high levels of human CD4 and coreceptors CCR5 and CXCR4 (Platt et al., 1998)
evidence: This describes the cell line used in the study, supported by citation.

claim: TZM-bl cells were incubated with 130 µg/mL of inhibitor and ~5000 TCID50/mL of HIV-1 pseudovirus at 37 °C for 2, 4, or 48 hr.
source: We conducted ET experiments by first incubating TZM-bl cells, a HeLa cell line that stably expresses high levels of human CD4 and coreceptors CCR5 and CXCR4 (Platt et al., 1998), with 130 µg/mL of inhibitor (either T1249-Fc, D5, or CPT31) and ~5000 TCID50/mL of HIV-1 pseudovirus at 37 °C for 2, 4, or 48 hr
evidence: This describes the experimental conditions used in the study.

claim: Pseudoviruses derived from two primary isolate HIV-1 strains were used: SC4226618 (Tier 2) and 6535 (Tier 1B).
source: In order to verify that results were not dependent upon a particular viral strain, we used pseudoviruses derived from two primary isolate HIV-1 strains: SC4226618 (Tier 2) and 6535 (Tier 1B) (Li et al., 2005)
evidence: This describes the viral strains used in the study, with citation.

claim: TZM-bl cells are contaminated with ecotropic murine leukemia virus (MLV).
source: TZM-bl cells are contaminated with ecotropic murine leukemia virus (Takeuchi et al., 2008), which does not affect their use for HIV-1 in vitro neutralization assays (Platt et al., 2009).
evidence: This is established knowledge about TZM-bl cells, supported by citations.

claim: MLV contamination does not affect the use of TZM-bl cells for HIV-1 in vitro neutralization assays.
source: TZM-bl cells are contaminated with ecotropic murine leukemia virus (Takeuchi et al., 2008), which does not affect their use for HIV-1 in vitro neutralization assays (Platt et al., 2009).
evidence: This is established knowledge, supported by citation.

claim: Budding MLV virions were occasionally observed in surveys of TZM-bl cells incubated in the presence or absence of fusion inhibitors.
source: In our surveys of TZM-bl cells incubated in the presence or absence of fusion inhibitors, we occasionally observed budding MLV virions (Figure 2—figure supplement 1b).
evidence: This is an observation from the experiments, shown in the figure supplement.

claim: MLV serves as a control for non-specific inhibition in TZM-bl–based HIV-1 in vitro neutralization assays.
source: As MLV serves as a control for non-specific inhibition in TZM-bl–based HIV-1 in vitro neutralization assays (Montefiori, 2005)
evidence: This is established knowledge about the use of MLV as a control, supported by citation.

claim: The fusion inhibitors used in the experiments have no effect on MLV fusion.
source: the fusion inhibitors used in our experiments are known to have no effect on MLV fusion, thus contaminating MLV virions were not captured during fusion in our experiments.
evidence: This is an inference based on the known specificity of the fusion inhibitors.

claim: Contaminating MLV virions were not captured during fusion in the experiments.
source: thus contaminating MLV virions were not captured during fusion in our experiments.
evidence: This is an inference based on the specificity of the fusion inhibitors.

claim: To identify attached virions by EM, the peripheries of TZM-bl cells were scanned to locate roughly spherical objects with diameters ~ 100 nm that were near a cell surface.
source: To identify attached virions by EM (Figure 2; Figure 2—figure supplement 1), the peripheries of TZM-bl cells were scanned to locate roughly spherical objects with diameters ~ 100 nm that were near a cell surface.
evidence: This describes the method used to identify attached virions.

claim: Regions of interest were examined at higher magnification and at tilts of 0°, 35° and −35° to verify that the objects were spherical.
source: Regions of interest were then examined at higher magnification and at tilts of 0°, 35° and −35° to verify that the objects were spherical, as expected for an HIV-1 virion (Figure 2—figure supplement 1c).
evidence: This describes the method used to verify that objects were virions.

claim: Potential virions were observed through a defocus series to detect core structures found inside authentic virions: a bullet-shaped core in mature HIV-1 and a C-shaped core in immature HIV-1.
source: Potential virions were then observed through a defocus series to detect core structures found inside authentic virions: that is a bullet-shaped core in mature HIV-1 and a C-shaped core in immature HIV-1 (Benjamin et al., 2005; Wright et al., 2007).
evidence: This describes the method used to verify that objects were virions, with citations.

claim: Control experiments in which pseudovirus and TZM-bl cells were incubated without inhibitor, with an irrelevant IgG, or with a low concentration of inhibitor, were prepared and analyzed in the same way.
source: Control experiments in which pseudovirus and TZM-bl cells were incubated without inhibitor, with an irrelevant IgG, or with a low concentration of inhibitor, were prepared and analyzed in the same way (Figure 2—figure supplement 1d).
evidence: This describes the control experiments performed.

claim: In surveys of TZM-bl cells treated with either SC4226618 or 6535 pseudovirus and 130 µg/mL of any of the three fusion inhibitors, virions were found attached to the surface of a TZM-bl cell by several (usually 2 or 3) narrow densities.
source: In surveys of TZM-bl cells treated with either SC4226618 or 6535 pseudovirus and 130 µg/mL of any of the three fusion inhibitors, we found virions that were attached to the surface of a TZM-bl cell by several (usually 2 or 3) narrow densities (Figures 2 and 3d; Figure 3—figure supplement 1; Figure 3—source data 1).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the experiments, shown in multiple figures.

claim: In control experiments with no inhibitor, an irrelevant Fc-containing protein, or T1249-Fc at 0.01x its IC50 value, no attached virions were found in examinations of >100 cells.
source: To verify that the attached virions resulted from treatment with a fusion inhibitor, we analyzed control experiments in which we incubated TZM-bl cells and pseudovirus with either no inhibitor, with an irrelevant Fc-containing protein (Z004, an anti-Zika virus IgG [Robbiani et al., 2017]), or with the T1249-Fc inhibitor at a concentration equivalent to 0.01x of its neutralization potency (i.e. its IC50 value) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1a). In examinations of >100 cells, we found no attached virions and also very few virions that were within a distance that could accommodate attachment.
evidence: This is data from control experiments showing specificity of the attachment to fusion inhibitor treatment.

claim: Very few virions were within a distance that could accommodate attachment in control experiments.
source: In examinations of >100 cells, we found no attached virions and also very few virions that were within a distance that could accommodate attachment.
evidence: This is an observation from control experiments.

claim: ET examination of the few cases (<20) in which virions were found adjacent to cells in control experiments confirmed that none of the virions were attached to a host cell membrane.
source: We used ET to examine the few cases (<20) in which we found virions adjacent to cells, which confirmed that none of the virions were attached to a host cell membrane (Figure 2—figure supplement 1d).
evidence: This is data from control experiments confirming the specificity of attachment.

claim: The approximate dimensions of the densities found for virions attached to TZM-bl cells in the presence of a fusion inhibitor were on average 15.6 ± 2.8 nm in length and 3.9 nm ±0.8 nm in thickness (n = 20).
source: The approximate dimensions of the densities found for virions attached to TZM-bl cells in the presence of a fusion inhibitor were on average 15.6 ± 2.8 nm in length and 3.9 nm ±0.8 nm in thickness (n = 20) (Figure 3a–c)
evidence: This is quantitative data from measurements of the attachment structures.

claim: The densities linking virions to cells are referred to as 'spokes' to distinguish them from the wider densities described as 'rods' in a previous ET study.
source: thus we refer to the densities as 'spokes' to distinguish them from the wider densities described as 'rods' in the previous ET study of virions attached to cells (Sougrat et al., 2007).
evidence: This is a nomenclature choice to distinguish from previous work.

claim: The spokes in the experiments resembled fusion intermediates observed in cryo-ET studies of hemagglutinin-mediated fusion of influenza virions with receptor-containing liposomes.
source: Interestingly, the spokes in our experiments, although imaged at relatively low resolution, resembled fusion intermediates observed in cryo-ET studies of hemagglutinin-mediated fusion of influenza virions with receptor-containing liposomes (Calder and Rosenthal, 2016)
evidence: This is a comparison to previous work on influenza fusion, supported by citation.

claim: The spokes resembled low pH-induced structural intermediates of hemagglutinin deduced from single-particle cryo-EM reconstructions.
source: and also low pH-induced structural intermediates of hemagglutinin deduced from single-particle cryo-EM reconstructions (Benton et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a comparison to previous work on hemagglutinin, supported by citation.

claim: In some samples incubated with D5 IgG, densities adjacent to one or more spokes were occasionally found that could represent the bound IgG.
source: In some of our samples incubated with the largest inhibitor (D5 IgG), we occasionally found densities adjacent to one or more spokes that could represent the bound IgG (Figure 2d).
evidence: This is an observation from the experiments, shown in Figure 2d.

claim: Virions attached with spokes were found on 10–30% of TZM-bl cells that were examined.
source: We found virions attached with spokes to 10–30% of TZM-bl cells that were examined, usually located on the thin leading edges of cells.
evidence: This is quantitative data about the frequency of attached virions.

claim: Attached virions were usually located on the thin leading edges of cells.
source: We found virions attached with spokes to 10–30% of TZM-bl cells that were examined, usually located on the thin leading edges of cells.
evidence: This is an observation about the location of attached virions.

claim: Most cells showed only one attached virion per 400 nm section, but occasional cells exhibited 3–5 attached virions.
source: Most cells showed only one attached virion per 400 nm section, but occasional cells exhibited 3–5 attached virions.
evidence: This is quantitative data about the number of attached virions per cell.

claim: The attachment sites were generally flat, as opposed to the target cell exhibiting a concave surface corresponding to the circumference of the virion.
source: The attachment sites were generally flat, as opposed to the target cell exhibiting a concave surface corresponding to the circumference of the virion as previously described (Sougrat et al., 2007)
evidence: This is an observation about the morphology of attachment sites, contrasted with previous work.

claim: Distances between spokes were ~7 nm to ~15 nm.
source: with distances of ~7 nm to ~15 nm between spokes.
evidence: This is quantitative data from measurements of attachment sites.

claim: The majority of attached virions were mature, as identified by their bullet-shaped cores.
source: The majority of attached virions were mature, as identified by their bullet-shaped cores (Figures 2–4)
evidence: This is an observation from the experiments, shown in multiple figures.

claim: A minor subset of attached virions (~5%) were immature.
source: but a minor subset of attached virions (~5%) were immature.
evidence: This is quantitative data about the maturation state of attached virions.

Indeed, Env trimers that did not participate in attachment were sometimes observed in tomographic slices (Figure 4). We hypothesized that more Envs might join in the attachment site if we used a virus in which Envs could exhibit increased lateral mobility in the viral membrane to allow Env diffusion to the attachment site. Increased Env mobility in the viral membrane has been described in viruses with an Env cytoplasmic tail deletion that eliminates interactions with the viral matrix protein (Crooks et al., 2008; Roy et al., 2013; Pezeshkian et al., 2019).
evidence: This is established knowledge from the literature, supported by multiple citations.
